--- filters: - naquiz format: html: toc: true toc-location: left toc-title: "In this session:" --- # Workshop 8: Machine Learning {#sec-workshop08} In this workshop, we will train, test and validate machine learning models. ::: {.callout-tip title="Learning Objectives"} This workshop directly builds on today's lecture. At the end of this session, learners should be able to: 1. Compare supervised ML domains, and explore their applications in biomedical research. 2. Construct a complete `tidymodels` workflow — preprocessing [recipe](wk11_fr.qmd#recipe){.quarto-xref}, model specification, and [workflow](wk11_fr.qmd#workflow){.quarto-xref} bundle — to train a random forest classifier 3. Explain the [train/test](wk11_fr.qmd#train-test-split){.quarto-xref} paradigm for supervised ML 4. Explain the key metrics for assessing performance: [confusion matrix](wk11_fr.qmd#confusion-matrix){.quarto-xref}, [AUROC, AUPRC](wk11_fr.qmd#auroc-auprc){.quarto-xref} ::: To explore additional concepts discussed in the lecture beyond this workshop, such as [hyperparameter tuning](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/tuning/) and [cross-validation](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/resampling/) for improving model quality, see the `tidymodels` tutorials linked throughout this page. ## Background {#sec-mlbackground .unnumbered} [Machine learning](wk11_fr.qmd#machine-learning){.quarto-xref} (ML) is an umbrella term that encompasses classical statistical methods, linear models (both simple and generalised), and non-parametric techniques such as decision trees, support vector machines, autoencoders, and neural networks. Each of these methods are called machine learning [engines](wk11_fr.qmd#engines){.quarto-xref} when used to train a [model](wk11_fr.qmd#model){.quarto-xref}. ML forms the foundation of [artificial intelligence](wk11_fr.qmd#artificial-intelligence){.quarto-xref}. For instance, large language models such as ChatGPT are trained using deep neural networks. Machine learning refers to the use of computers (machines) to identify statistical trends in data and store those trends/relationships in a model. The process of identifying trends ([learning](wk11_fr.qmd#learning){.quarto-xref}) and then predicting features of newly provided data ([predicting](wk11_fr.qmd#predicting){.quarto-xref}) is common to all ML workflows. ::: {.callout-note title="Does your machine need supervision?"} ML used to predict the status (label) of new samples is termed [supervised ML](wk11_fr.qmd#supervised-ml){.quarto-xref}. In [unsupervised ML](wk11_fr.qmd#unsupervised-ml){.quarto-xref}, the model is trained on data without labels. The model tries to find patterns, groupings, or structures in the data, often by performing pair-wise sample similarity tests. This is useful when we don't know the categories in advance, such as clustering patients based on gene expression profiles, or identifying hidden patterns in imaging data. We will be learning more about this in [Tutorial 11](@sec-tute11). Comparing 'data-driven' groupings to existing category labels can either confirm existing categories or provide evidence for revising them. [Principal components analysis](wk11_fr.qmd#pca){.quarto-xref}, [multidimensional scaling](wk11_fr.qmd#mds){.quarto-xref} and [tree-based clustering](wk11_fr.qmd#tree-clustering){.quarto-xref} algorithms are examples of unsupervised ML. ::: ## Biomedical Context {#sec-mlcontext .unnumbered} ML has many exciting applications in biomedical research. As you saw in the ML lecture, unsupervised and supervised ML workflows can be used on histological (imaging) features of tissue slices, with matched labels indicating whether the tissue is healthy/benign or malignant (cancerous) @zhu2016. Another example of how ML can be used in this context is to identify whether patients infected with malaria are seropositive/seronegative based on specific anti-malaria IgG antibody levels @longley2020. ## Terminology {#sec-mlterms .unnumbered} In training ML models, the machine 'learns from the training dataset' and 'predicts the validation dataset'. The accuracy of the predictions on the validation data is used to update the model (known as 'reinforcement learning'). Once the model has been trained, it is tested on a 'hold-out' or 'test' dataset, which has not been used at any point in training or validation. The accuracy of performance on the test set is the ultimate test of the 'predictive value' of a model — that is, how valuable it is for informing real-world decisions. ## Tidymodels packages {#sec-mlpackages .unnumbered} [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/) is an R package that encompasses multiple sub-packages, all of which work together with tidy data! This means they seamlessly "pipe" in with our dplyr and ggplot2 functions that we've come to know very well over this course. In the past, each ML engine was siloed in its own package, with unique functions and arguments. `tidymodels` provides a consistent user experience for data pre-processing, training, validation, model tuning and prediction, and allows us to switch between ML engines quickly and easily! Its sister package [tidyclust](https://tidyclust.tidymodels.org/) extends the same interface to unsupervised machine learning models — we will use it for clustering in [Tutorial 11](@sec-tute11). ::: {.callout-note title="Further reading"} To learn more about machine learning in R, check out the excellent book [Tidy Modelling with R](https://www.tmwr.org) ::: # Random Forest Classification with tidymodels {#sec-w8-supervised} ::: {.callout-tip title="Learning Objectives"} **Aim:** Train a supervised machine learning model (classifier) to predict mouse strain based on physiological features. **Methods:** 1. Explore the data 2. Train a machine learning model using pre-defined [hyperparameters](wk11_fr.qmd#hyperparameter){.quarto-xref} 3. Test the model and evaluate its performance ::: ## Setup {#sec-mlsetup} ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Install packages if not already installed install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger")) # vip was recently removed from CRAN where packages live, # so install the last CRAN version (0.4.1) from the CRAN archive install.packages( "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/vip/vip_0.4.1.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source" ) library(tidyverse) # Data manipulation and visualisation library(tidymodels) # Modelling framework library(ranger) # Random forest engine library(vip) # Variable importance plots ``` ::: Our `mice` dataset is clean and well-separated — almost too clean. It's a great teaching dataset, but real-world data is rarely this tidy. To give a more realistic sense of how ML performs on messier data, we use a noisy version of the dataset, `noisy_dosage`, created by adding random measurement error to the physiological features. {{< downloadthis data/noisy_mousezempic_dosage_data.csv dname=noisy_mousezempic_dosage_data label="Download data for this session" icon=file-earmark-arrow-down type=primary class=data-button id=workshop_data >}} Save into your `data/` directory. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} noisy_dosage <- read_csv( "data/noisy_mousezempic_dosage_data.csv" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 333 Columns: 7 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (3): mouse_strain, sex, cage_number dbl (4): weight_lost_g, drug_dose_g, tail_length_mm, initial_weight_g ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ::: Or you can run the code below to download the dataset from a URL: ::: {.cell exec='false'} ```{.r .cell-code} noisy_dosage <- read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WEHI-Education/BIOL90042_R_Course/refs/heads/main/data/noisy_mousezempic_dosage_data.csv" ) ``` ::: ## Split Data into Training & Testing Sets {#sec-rsample} As we are now employing a **supervised ML** algorithm, we split our `noisy_dosage` dataset into two distinct datasets: train and test. We train the model on the training set and evaluate it on the test set. The test set must **never** be seen during model training or tuning — this is what allows it to give an unbiased estimate of real-world performance. We use a 75/25 train/test split (`prop = 0.75`) and stratify by strain (`strata = mouse_strain`) so that each set has proportional representation of all three strain. To do this reproducibly and to keep our results consistent, we need to first set a seed. :::{.callout-note} ## What is a seed, and why do we set one? Many steps in machine learning involve **randomness** — for example, randomly assigning samples to train/test sets, or the random choices a random forest makes while growing its trees. By default, R generates *different* random numbers every time, so the same code can give slightly different results each time it runs. `set.seed()` fixes the starting point of R's random number generator. Setting a seed means that **anyone, on any computer, in any session**, who runs the same code will get **exactly the same results** — which is essential for reproducible science. Two things to know: - The number itself is arbitrary (`123`, `2026`, anything) — what matters is that you pick one and don't change it. - It is best practice to set a seed **immediately before** each step that uses randomness, e.g. before `initial_split()` and before `last_fit()`. If you re-run a later chunk on its own without re-setting the seed, your results may differ from a full top-to- bottom run. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # set a seed set.seed(123) # create our 75/25 train/test split and stratify by strain dosage_split <- initial_split( noisy_dosage, prop = 0.75, strata = mouse_strain ) # subset our datasets to use in this analysis dosage_train <- training(dosage_split) dosage_test <- testing(dosage_split) ``` ::: Great. Now let's confirm that our stratification was respected by inspecting our train and test datasets for their proportion of each strain. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_check <- dosage_train %>% group_by(mouse_strain) %>% summarise(n_strain = n()) %>% mutate(set = "train", proportion = n_strain / sum(n_strain)) test_check <- dosage_test %>% group_by(mouse_strain) %>% summarise(n_strain = n()) %>% mutate(set = "test", proportion = n_strain / sum(n_strain)) bind_rows( train_check, test_check, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 4 mouse_strain n_strain set proportion 1 BALBc 51 train 0.205 2 Black6 89 train 0.357 3 CD1 109 train 0.438 4 BALBc 17 test 0.202 5 Black6 30 test 0.357 6 CD1 37 test 0.440 ``` ::: ::: Now that our data is split, we follow the standard `tidymodels` modelling sequence: define a recipe, specify a model and engine, bundle these into a workflow, and fit the model. ::: {.callout-note title="An alternative to a single train/test split"} Instead of a single train/test split, we could train on the entire dataset and estimate performance using repeated [cross-validation](wk11_fr.qmd#cross-validation){.quarto-xref}, which reduces the bias introduced by any one particular split. See the tidymodels [cross-validation tutorial](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/resampling/) for a worked example of this approach. ::: ::::::::: {.callout-important title="Test Your Knowledge"} :::::::: question Why must the test set never be used during model training? ::::::: choices ::: choice It slows down computation too much to be practical ::: ::: {.choice .correct-choice} Using it during training would let information leak into the fitting process, giving an overly optimistic estimate of real-world performance ::: ::: choice The test set always contains different variables to the training set ::: ::: choice It is only a concern for regression models, not classification ::: ::::::: ::::::::
Solutions

1. Computation time is not the reason for the train/test split — it exists to give an honest estimate of performance. 2. Correct! If the model (or its tuning process) ever sees the test set, performance estimates become biased ('data leakage') and no longer reflect how the model will perform on genuinely new data. 3. The test set contains the same variables as the training set — only the *observations* differ. 4. The train/test paradigm applies equally to regression and classification tasks.

::::::::: ## Define a Preprocessing Recipe {#sec-recipe} The **[recipe](wk11_fr.qmd#recipe){.quarto-xref}** specifies which variables (columns) we want to include in our model and what preprocessing steps should be applied to them, expressed as a statistical formula: `outcome variable ~ predictor variables`. ::: {.cell exec='false'} ```{.r .cell-code} recipe( # your recipe in outcome variable ~ predictor variables (all) mouse_strain ~ ., # remember: we create our model on the training dataset only data = dosage_train ) ``` ::: As this is a **supervised ML** workflow, we specify `mouse_strain` as the outcome variable in the recipe formula, and keep all remaining columns as predictor variables by using `.` on the right-hand side. We can add pre-processing steps using the `step_*` functions in the `recipes` R package. Examples of pre-processing functions include: - `step_corr()` can remove correlated predictors from your recipe so that redundant variables carrying the same information are dropped. Highly correlated predictors can inflate model variance and make feature importance estimates unstable. - `step_dummy()` converts categorical predictors (`sex`, `cage_number`) into one-hot encoded numeric columns, since most ML engines require numeric inputs. - `step_log()` converts numeric values to their logarithm, which can help reduce the impact of large values in the data. - `step_normalize()` can scale numeric predictors to mean = 0, sd = 1. This ensures that a variable with a large numeric range does not dominate a variable with a small range simply because of its scale. - `step_sqrt()` applies a square-root transformation to numeric predictors, which compresses large values to reduce right-skewness and the influence of extreme observations. - `step_naomit()`, `step_mutate()`, `step_filter()` and other dplyr-style verbs let you tidy your data inside the recipe (e.g. dropping rows with missing values or creating new columns) so that the same transformations are applied consistently to both the training and test sets, preventing data leakage. Note that: - `all_nominal_predictors()` can be used inside e.g. `step_dummy()` to apply that step to all nominal (or categorical) predictor variables in the recipe. - `all_numeric_predictors()` can be used inside e.g. `step_log()`, `step_normalise()`, `step_sqrt()` to apply that step to all numeric predictor variables in the recipe. For our dataset, we will add two preprocessing steps: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dosage_recipe <- recipe(mouse_strain ~ ., data = dosage_train) %>% # we will use step_normalize(): # put all numeric predictors on a comparable scale (mean 0, # sd 1) so differences in units — e.g. drug dose vs weight # lost — don't bias the model step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>% # we will use step_dummy(): # convert categorical predictors (e.g. sex, cage_number) into # numeric columns, since most ML engines only accept numeric inputs step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) summary(dosage_recipe) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7 × 4 variable type role source 1 weight_lost_g predictor original 2 drug_dose_g predictor original 3 tail_length_mm predictor original 4 initial_weight_g predictor original 5 sex predictor original 6 cage_number predictor original 7 mouse_strain outcome original ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Curious about redundant predictors?"} We use **all** four physiological features here without checking whether any are redundant. See the tidymodels [Feature Engineering and Selection](https://www.tidymodels.org/books/fes/) book for a discussion of checking for correlated predictors and reducing dimensionality. ::: ## Specify the Random Forest Model {#sec-parsnip-model} A random forest is built from many individual **decision trees**. A single decision tree makes a prediction by asking a series of yes/no questions about the predictors, splitting the data at each step until it reaches a decision. For example, a bank might decide whether to approve a loan by first checking an applicant's credit history, then their income (@fig-decision-tree, left). The same logic applies in a biological context: a tree could classify a sample as disease-positive or -negative based on the expression levels of a few genes (@fig-decision-tree, right). ![A single decision tree splits on predictors in sequence to reach a decision: illustrated here for a loan approval example (left) and a gene-expression-based disease classification example (right).](images/S08F01_RF_tree_1.png){#fig-decision-tree} ::: {.callout-tip title="What is a Random Forest?"} A single decision tree can easily overfit its training data. A [random forest](wk11_fr.qmd#random-forest){.quarto-xref} addresses this by growing an **ensemble** of many decision trees, each on a random bootstrap sample of the data, considering only a random subset of predictors at each split (`mtry`). This makes the trees independent and uncorrelated with one another. Every tree "votes" on the predicted class, and the forest's final prediction is simply the **majority vote** across all trees (@fig-random-forest), typically giving more accurate and stable predictions than any single tree. ::: ![A random forest grows many independent, uncorrelated decision trees from the same data and takes a majority vote across trees to arrive at the final predicted class.](images/S08F02_RF_tree_2.png){#fig-random-forest} Below we specify the random forest model. We use the default hyperparameters for `mtry` and `min_n`, and fix the number of trees at 500 (`trees = 500`). If you'd like to see how to systematically search for better hyperparameter values, see the tidymodels [hyperparameter tuning tutorial](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/tuning/). For the engine, we use the [`ranger`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ranger) R package, and set `importance = "impurity"` so that we can later calculate variable importance, which is a measure of how much each predictor contributes to classification accuracy. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rf_model <- rand_forest(trees = 500) %>% set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>% set_mode("classification") rf_model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Random Forest Model Specification (classification) Main Arguments: trees = 500 Engine-Specific Arguments: importance = impurity Computational engine: ranger ``` ::: ::: ## Bundle into a Workflow {#sec-workflows} We now combine the recipe and model into a single **[workflow](wk11_fr.qmd#workflow){.quarto-xref}** object. Bundling them together ensures that the same preprocessing steps are always applied consistently whenever the model is fitted or used to predict — reducing the risk of errors and making the pipeline reproducible. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Combine the recipe and model into a workflow rf_workflow <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(dosage_recipe) %>% add_model(rf_model) rf_workflow ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ══ Workflow ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Preprocessor: Recipe Model: rand_forest() ── Preprocessor ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 2 Recipe Steps • step_normalize() • step_dummy() ── Model ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Random Forest Model Specification (classification) Main Arguments: trees = 500 Engine-Specific Arguments: importance = impurity Computational engine: ranger ``` ::: ::: ## Fit the Model {#sec-parsnip-fit} We now fit the final model on the full training set and evaluate it on the test set. The `last_fit()` function fits the workflow once on the training data and generates predictions on the held-out test set in a single step. Recall that the test set has not been seen during training or tuning. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Set a new seed set.seed(456) # Fit model on the training data and generate predictions on test data final_fit <- last_fit(rf_workflow, dosage_split) # Visualise the results of model fitting final_fit ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Resampling results # Manual resampling # A tibble: 1 × 6 splits id .metrics .notes .predictions .workflow 1 train/test split ``` ::: ::: The output of `final_fit` doesn't actually tell us much. It says that we have successfully fitted a random forest model to the training data, and that predictions were generated on the test set, but it gives no indication of how well the model actually performed. All we have at this point is confirmation that the workflow ran end-to-end: the resampling split was applied, the recipe was prepped, the model was trained on the 249 training mice, and predictions were made for the 84 held-out test mice. To judge whether our model is any good, we need to interrogate this fitted object further. The next step is to explicitly collect the performance metrics stored inside `final_fit` and evaluate the model's predictions against the true test set labels. ## Evaluate Model Performance {#sec-tune-yardstick} We can collect the test set performance metrics using `collect_metrics()`. By default this reports `accuracy` (the proportion of correctly classified mice), `roc_auc` (AUROC, the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) and `brier_class` (the Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted class probabilities and true outcomes, lower values indicate better calibrated probability predictions). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} collect_metrics(final_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 .metric .estimator .estimate .config 1 accuracy multiclass 0.917 pre0_mod0_post0 2 roc_auc hand_till 0.969 pre0_mod0_post0 3 brier_class multiclass 0.0871 pre0_mod0_post0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Practice exercise: Increasing number of trees in our forest"} What would happen if we increased the number of trees in our random forest? Create a random forest model now with `trees = 5000`, using the `ranger` engine and `"classification"` mode. Save this into a new model object and collect the metrics using `collect_metrics()`. Compare this with `final_fit`.
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create our new model with 5,000 trees rf_trees_model <- rand_forest(trees = 5000) %>% set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>% set_mode("classification") # Bundle into a workflow rf_trees_workflow <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(dosage_recipe) %>% add_model(rf_trees_model) # Fit the workflow to the training data (using same seed) rf_trees_fit <- last_fit(rf_trees_workflow, dosage_split) # Evaluate model performance of new model collect_metrics(rf_trees_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 .metric .estimator .estimate .config 1 accuracy multiclass 0.917 pre0_mod0_post0 2 roc_auc hand_till 0.970 pre0_mod0_post0 3 brier_class multiclass 0.0849 pre0_mod0_post0 ``` ::: ::: In this case, `accuracy` is almost the same as the previous model. The `roc_auc` improved from 0.969 (`final_fit`) to 0.971 (`rf_trees_fit`). The brier class was lower in `rf_trees_fit` compared to `final_fit`, indicating better probability predictions. This is expected: as we increase the number of trees in a random forest, predictions are averaged over more trees, reducing variance and giving slightly more stable and accurate probability estimates. However, the gains are typically small beyond a few hundred trees, and training time increases accordingly.
::: We can also visualise performance using precision-recall (PR) and ROC curves. Since `mouse_strain` has three classes, `pr_curve()` and `roc_curve()` use a **one-vs-all** strategy, treating each strain in turn as the positive class against the other two. :::{.callout-note title="What do the Precision-Recall and Receiver Operating Characteristic Curves show us?"} ![Two side-by-side plots comparing three classifier models (A, B, and C) of differing quality. Left: a precision-recall curve with recall (0 to 1) on the x-axis and precision (0 to 1) on the y-axis. Right: an ROC curve with 1 - specificity (false positive rate, 0 to 1) on the x-axis and sensitivity (true positive rate, 0 to 1) on the y-axis, with a dashed diagonal line representing chance performance.](images/S08F03_PRC_ROC.png) PR curves (Left) show the trade-off between **precision** (y-axis; e.g., out of all the mice classified as CD1, how many were actually CD1?) and **recall** or sensitivity (x-axis; e.g., out of all the real CD1 mice in the dataset, how many did the model successfully classify?) as the classification threshold varies. ROC curves (Right) plot the **true positive rate** or sensitivity (y-axis; e.g., out of all the real CD1 mice in the dataset, how many did the model successfully classify?) against the **false positive rate** or 1 - specificity (x-axis; e.g., out of all the non-CD1 mice in the dataset, how many did the model wrongly mistake for CD1?) as the classification threshold varies. A curve that bows toward the top-left corner indicates better discrimination between classes, and an AUC closer to 1.0 indicates better overall classification performance. ::: ### Precision-Recall Curve {#sec-prc} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% pr_curve( truth = mouse_strain, .pred_BALBc, .pred_Black6, .pred_CD1 ) %>% autoplot() + labs(title = "PR Curves: Random Forest (Test Set)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workshop_8_files/figure-html/aupr-curve-1.png){width=2000} ::: ::: In this graph, we can see that the model maintains high precision even as recall increases, meaning it identifies most positive cases while keeping the number of false positives low. A curve that stays near the top-right corner indicates strong performance; the baseline for a "no-skill" classifier is the prevalence of the positive class, not 0.5 as with AUROC. ::: {.callout-important title="Practice exercise: Increasing number of trees in our forest: PR Curves"} Using the `rf_trees_fit` fitted model with 5,000 trees instead of 500 trees in `final_fit`, now evaluate the PR curve. How does this impact the PR curve?
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rf_trees_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% pr_curve( truth = mouse_strain, .pred_BALBc, .pred_Black6, .pred_CD1 ) %>% autoplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workshop_8_files/figure-html/compare-with-more-trees-2-1.png){width=2000} ::: ::: The PR curve is nearly identical to the one generated from `final_fit` with 500 trees. Increasing the number of trees from 500 to 5,000 does not meaningfully change the precision-recall trade-off: both curves hug the top-right corner, maintaining high precision across the full range of recall for all three strains. This is consistent with the metrics we compared earlier: once a random forest has enough trees for predictions to stabilise, adding more trees yields only marginal improvements, since predictions are already averaged over a large ensemble. The main cost of the extra trees is computation time, not model performance.
::: We can also calculate the Area under the PR Curve (AUPRC) using the `final_fit` object. The AUPRC value represents the area under the PR curve and provides a single value to summarize the model's performance across all classification thresholds. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate AUPRC (one-vs-all per strain class) final_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% pr_auc( truth = mouse_strain, .pred_BALBc, .pred_Black6, .pred_CD1 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 pr_auc macro 0.928 ``` ::: ::: An AUPRC of 0.927 indicates the model maintains high precision across most recall levels for each strain — strong positive-class performance. ::::::::: {.callout-important title="Test Your Knowledge"} :::::::: question Looking at the PR curves and AUPRC for each mouse strain in `final_fit`, which class does the model predict best? ::::::: choices ::: {.choice .correct-choice} Black6 is predicted best (its curve stays closest to the top-right corner) ::: ::: choice BALBc is predicted best because its curve has the highest baseline ::: ::: choice All three strains are predicted equally well, since they come from the same random forest model ::: ::: choice CD1 is predicted best because it has the highest prevalence in the test set ::: ::::::: ::::::::
Solutions

1. Correct! Black6's PR curve stays nearest the top-right corner (AUPR ≈ 0.999), indicating the model identifies Black6 mice with both high precision and high recall. BALBc is the least prevalent class (~20% of the test set), and with fewer positive cases its precision estimates are noisier and the curve less stable. 2. Incorrect — BALBc actually has the *lowest* AUPR (~0.84) of the three strains, and a low prevalence lowers, not raises, the baseline of a PR curve. 3. Incorrect — a single model can perform very differently across classes, especially when class frequencies are imbalanced. 4. Incorrect — while CD1 is the most prevalent class, its curve sits below Black6's; prevalence alone does not determine predictive performance.

::::::::: ### Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve {#sec-roc} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% roc_curve( truth = mouse_strain, .pred_BALBc, .pred_Black6, .pred_CD1 ) %>% autoplot() + labs(title = "ROC Curves: Random Forest (Test Set)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workshop_8_files/figure-html/auroc-curve-1.png){width=2000} ::: ::: Because `mouse_strain` has three classes, this produces one curve per strain (each treating that strain vs. the other two) rather than a single combined curve. Here we can see that our ROC curves are all within the top left-hand corner, so that's great. ::: {.callout-important title="Practice exercise: Increasing number of trees in our forest: ROC Curves"} Using the `rf_trees_fit` fitted model with 5,000 trees instead of 500 trees in `final_fit`, now evaluate the ROC curve. How does this impact the ROC curve?
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rf_trees_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% roc_curve( truth = mouse_strain, .pred_BALBc, .pred_Black6, .pred_CD1 ) %>% autoplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workshop_8_files/figure-html/compare-with-more-trees-3-1.png){width=2000} ::: ::: The ROC curve is nearly identical to the one generated from `final_fit` with 500 trees. Increasing the number of trees from 500 to 5,000 does not meaningfully change the sensitivity-specificity trade-off: both curves hug the top-left corner, maintaining high sensitivity across almost the full range of specificity for all three strains. This is consistent with the metrics we compared earlier (`roc_auc` of 0.969 vs 0.971).
::: As with the PR curve and AUPCR, we can calculate the AUROC for our ROC curve. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate AUROC for our ROC curve final_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% roc_auc( truth = mouse_strain, .pred_BALBc, .pred_Black6, .pred_CD1 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 roc_auc hand_till 0.969 ``` ::: ::: The AUC for this model is 0.971 which is a very strong indicator of model classification performance. ::::::::: {.callout-important title="Test Your Knowledge"} :::::::: question Looking at the ROC curves and AUROC for each mouse strain in `final_fit`, which class does the model predict best? ::::::: choices ::: choice BALBc is predicted best because it is the least prevalent class ::: ::: choice All three strains are predicted equally well, since they come from the same random forest model ::: ::: {.choice .correct-choice} Black6 is predicted best (its curve stays closest to the top-left corner) ::: ::: choice CD1 is predicted best because it has the highest prevalence in the test set ::: ::::::: ::::::::
Solutions

1. Incorrect — BALBc actually has the *lowest* AUROC (~0.96, roughly tied with CD1). Unlike a PR curve, the ROC curve's no-skill baseline is the diagonal line regardless of prevalence, and low prevalence does not make performance better. 2. Incorrect — a single model can perform very differently across classes, especially when class frequencies are imbalanced. 3. Correct! Black6's ROC curve stays nearest the top-left corner (AUROC ≈ 0.999), indicating the model identifies Black6 mice with both high sensitivity and high specificity across almost all classification thresholds. 4. Incorrect — while CD1 is the most prevalent class, its curve sits below Black6's (AUROC ≈ 0.96 vs 0.999); prevalence alone does not determine predictive performance.

::::::::: ### Confusion Matrix {#sec-confmat} We can also evaluate the confusion matrix (`conf_mat()`), where rows are our "truth" (the strain in `noisy_dosage`; `truth = mouse_strain`) and columns are the "predictions" (the predicted strain; `estimate = .pred_class`). Diagonal cells are correct predictions, while off-diagonal cells are misclassifications. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% conf_mat( truth = mouse_strain, estimate = .pred_class ) %>% autoplot(type = "heatmap") + labs(title = "Confusion Matrix: Random Forest (Test Set)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workshop_8_files/figure-html/confusion-matrix-1.png){width=2000} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Practice exercise: Increasing number of trees in our forest: Confusion Matrix"} Using the `rf_trees_fit` fitted model with 5,000 trees instead of 500 trees in `final_fit`, now evaluate the confusion matrix. How does this impact the confusion matrix results?
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rf_trees_fit %>% collect_predictions() %>% conf_mat( truth = mouse_strain, estimate = .pred_class ) %>% autoplot(type = "heatmap") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workshop_8_files/figure-html/compare-with-more-trees-4-1.png){width=2000} ::: ::: The confusion matrix is essentially unchanged: with 5,000 trees we see the same pattern of (mostly diagonal) correct predictions and the same small number of misclassifications as with 500 trees. Both models correctly identify all 29 Black6 mice, while the few errors remain concentrated between BALBc and CD1 — the two strains whose predicted probabilities overlapped most in our earlier plots. This illustrates an important property of random forests: performance generally does not keep improving as we add more trees. Each tree in the forest is built slightly differently, and once we have enough trees, averaging their predictions together gives a stable result — extra trees just average into more of the same rather than adding new information. Increasing `trees` from 500 to 5,000 therefore has little effect on the confusion matrix (here the overall accuracy is identical, with AUROC increasing only marginally from ~0.969 to ~0.971), while costing roughly 10x the computation time. Random forests also do not overfit as more trees are added, so in practice we choose a number of trees that is "large enough" for the predictions to stabilise, rather than tuning it like other hyperparameters.
::: ::: {.callout-note title="Try it yourself"} Using `collect_predictions(final_fit)`, compute the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) for each strain class (see the `yardstick` package functions: `sens()`, `spec()`, `ppv()`, `npv()`). The tidymodels [cross-validation tutorial](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/resampling/) works through a similar calculation in detail if you'd like a worked example.
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} preds <- final_fit %>% collect_predictions() # Sensitivity (recall): proportion of actual positives correctly identified sens(preds, truth = mouse_strain, estimate = .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 sens macro 0.903 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Specificity: proportion of actual negatives correctly identified spec(preds, truth = mouse_strain, estimate = .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 spec macro 0.956 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Positive predictive value (precision): proportion of positive predictions that are correct ppv(preds, truth = mouse_strain, estimate = .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 ppv macro 0.912 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Negative predictive value: proportion of negative predictions that are correct npv(preds, truth = mouse_strain, estimate = .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 npv macro 0.957 ``` ::: ::: With more than two classes, these functions compute each metric using a "one-vs-rest" approach for every class and then return the macro-averaged result (the default `estimator = "macro"`). You can also compute all four metrics at once with `metric_set()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class_metrics <- metric_set(sens, spec, ppv, npv) class_metrics( preds, truth = mouse_strain, estimate = .pred_class ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 sens macro 0.903 2 spec macro 0.956 3 ppv macro 0.912 4 npv macro 0.957 ``` ::: ::: Here, all four metrics are very high, consistent with the nearly-diagonal confusion matrix we saw earlier.
::: ::::::::: {.callout-important title="Test Your Knowledge"} :::::::: question A classifier has an AUROC of 0.90 but an AUPRC of only 0.30. What does this most likely indicate? ::::::: choices ::: choice The model is performing extremely well overall, with no concerns ::: ::: {.choice .correct-choice} The classes in the dataset are likely imbalanced — AUPRC is more sensitive to class imbalance than AUROC ::: ::: choice AUPRC and AUROC should always be equal, so this must be a coding error ::: ::: choice The confusion matrix is no longer needed once you have an AUROC value ::: ::::::: ::::::::
Solutions

1. A high AUROC alongside a low AUPRC is a red flag, not a sign of strong performance — it usually means the model looks good on paper but struggles with the minority class. 2. Correct! As shown in the lecture's imbalanced-data example, AUROC can remain high under class imbalance while AUPRC drops sharply, because AUPRC is sensitive to how rare the positive class is. 3. These two metrics measure different trade-offs (sensitivity/specificity vs precision/recall) and are not expected to match. 4. The confusion matrix, AUROC and AUPRC each reveal different aspects of performance and are best used together.

::::::::: ## Variable Importance Plot {#sec-var} You may be interested in understanding which predictor variable was the most important in informing the final classification prediction. We can do this by extracting the fitted model (`extract_fit_parsnip()`) and plotting variable importance using the `vip` R package. Importance is measured by mean decrease in node impurity (Gini impurity), where higher values indicate a greater contribution to classification decisions. This tells us which physiological features best distinguish strains. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_fit %>% extract_fit_parsnip() %>% vip() + labs(title = "Variable Importance: Random Forest") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workshop_8_files/figure-html/variable-importance-1.png){width=2000} ::: ::: Here we can see that `initial_weight_g` is the most important variable that informs our random forest, and `sex` as the least informative variable! ## Predict Strain for the Synthetic Unlabelled Dataset {#sec-apply-models} Now that we have a trained and evaluated model, we can use it to predict on genuinely new data — this is often the ultimate goal of training an ML model. First, let's save our trained model so that we can apply it to this new unseen dataset. ::: {.cell exec='false'} ```{.r .cell-code} saveRDS(final_fit, "model/dosage.rds") ``` ::: Now, let's load in our new, unlabelled dataset, `new_dosage`, containing physiological measurements but **no strain labels**. {{< downloadthis data/new_mousezempic_dosage_data.csv dname=new_mousezempic_dosage_data label="Download new data for this session" icon=file-earmark-arrow-down type=primary class=data-button id=workshop_data >}} Save into your `data/` directory. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} new_dosage <- read_csv("data/new_mousezempic_dosage_data.csv") %>% # Convert character columns to factors to match the training data's # column types: step_dummy() in the recipe expects factor predictors mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 26 Columns: 7 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (2): cage_number, sex dbl (5): mouse_id, weight_lost_g, drug_dose_g, tail_length_mm, initial_weight_g ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ::: Or you can run the code below to download the dataset from a URL: ::: {.cell exec='false'} ```{.r .cell-code} new_dosage <- read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WEHI-Education/BIOL90042_R_Course/refs/heads/main/data/new_mousezempic_dosage_data.csv" ) %>% # Convert character columns to factors to match the training data's # column types: step_dummy() in the recipe expects factor predictors mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) ``` ::: Because we created this model in our working R session, we can use the `extract_workflow()` function on the `final_fit` object to simply extract the workflow and apply it to the dataset: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Extract the final fitted model from last_fit() final_model <- extract_workflow(final_fit) ``` ::: But it is often the case where we are applying the model in new R sessions or we give this to a collaborator for them to use. In this case, we will use our `model/dosage.rds` file that we saved and then the `extract_workflow()` function: ::: {.cell exec='false'} ```{.r .cell-code} loaded_model <- readRDS("model/dosage.rds") final_model <- extract_workflow(loaded_model) ``` ::: Now let's apply the model to our new dataset `new_dosage`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Generate class predictions and class probabilities new_predictions <- new_dosage %>% bind_cols( # generate class predictions predict(final_model, new_data = new_dosage), # generate class probabilities predict(final_model, new_data = new_dosage, type = "prob") ) # View predictions with confidence probabilities head(new_predictions, 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 11 mouse_id cage_number weight_lost_g drug_dose_g tail_length_mm 1 1 1A 2.5 0.00222 17.2 2 2 2B 4.23 0.00219 17 3 3 2B 4.39 0.00196 13.8 4 4 3E 3.06 0.00215 18.8 5 5 1A 4.57 0.00194 17.4 6 6 2B 4.19 0.0019 18.3 7 7 3E 2.88 0.00209 18.3 8 8 2B 4.84 0.00183 19.3 9 9 3E 4.56 0.00185 17.8 10 10 2B 5.14 0.00214 18.6 # ℹ 6 more variables: initial_weight_g , sex , .pred_class , # .pred_BALBc , .pred_Black6 , .pred_CD1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Functions: Convenience is key!"} It's often useful to wrap this prediction logic into a **reusable function**, so you (or a collaborator) can apply the saved model to any new dataset without repeating the code above. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Save the fitted model so it can be reloaded without re-training predict_mice <- function(df, model = "model/dosage.rds") { # Match the column types used during training df <- df %>% mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) # Load the saved model final_fit <- readRDS(model) # Extract the fitted workflow from last_fit() final_model <- extract_workflow(final_fit) # Generate class predictions and class probabilities df %>% bind_cols( predict(final_model, new_data = df), predict(final_model, new_data = df, type = "prob") ) } predict_mice(new_dosage) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 26 × 11 mouse_id cage_number weight_lost_g drug_dose_g tail_length_mm 1 1 1A 2.5 0.00222 17.2 2 2 2B 4.23 0.00219 17 3 3 2B 4.39 0.00196 13.8 4 4 3E 3.06 0.00215 18.8 5 5 1A 4.57 0.00194 17.4 6 6 2B 4.19 0.0019 18.3 7 7 3E 2.88 0.00209 18.3 8 8 2B 4.84 0.00183 19.3 9 9 3E 4.56 0.00185 17.8 10 10 2B 5.14 0.00214 18.6 # ℹ 16 more rows # ℹ 6 more variables: initial_weight_g , sex , .pred_class , # .pred_BALBc , .pred_Black6 , .pred_CD1 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Summary {#sec-w8-summary} Today we've learned the fundamental principles of machine learning in R, specifically using the `tidymodels` R packages to develop a **supervised** machine learning **classification** model. Here is a quick summary of what we've learnt: - The difference between **supervised** and **unsupervised** machine learning, and where **classification** fits in - The `tidymodels` ecosystem for building machine learning models in R - Splitting data into **training** and **testing** sets with `rsample`, using `set.seed()` for reproducibility and **stratified** sampling to preserve class balance - Defining preprocessing steps in a **recipe** (`recipes`) so the same transformations are applied consistently to training and test data - Specifying a **random forest** classification model with `parsnip` and bundling it with the recipe into a **workflow** (`workflows`) - Fitting the model on the training data with `last_fit()` and evaluating its performance on held-out test data - Assessing classification performance using **accuracy**, **precision– recall curves (AUPRC)**, **ROC curves (AUROC)**, **confusion matrices**, and per-class metrics like **sensitivity**, **specificity**, **PPV** and **NPV** (`yardstick`) - Using **variable importance plots** (`vip`) to identify which predictors drive the model's decisions - Saving a fitted model (`saveRDS()`), reloading it, and applying it to **predict classes and class probabilities** on new, unlabelled data — including wrapping the prediction logic in a reusable function You can download the summary sheet from this workshop here: {{< downloadthis resources/session_8_summary_sheet.pdf dname="session_8_summary_sheet" label="Download the summary sheet for workshop 8" icon="file-earmark-arrow-down" type="primary" class="data-button" id="summarysheet" >}} In Tutorial 11, you will apply the same recipe–model–workflow concepts to **unsupervised** machine learning, using k-means clustering to discover groupings in **unlabelled** data. If you'd like to learn more, look at the [further reading](wk11_fr.qmd) for this week, which includes links to `tidymodels` resources that can help for steps **not** covered in this workshop such as hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation.
